As a .sql file identical in structure to a model

questions.q: According to the real DAG diagram in this lesson, what do the green nodes represent, versus the blue node?
options: Green nodes are raw sources with no upstream dependency; the blue node is a model built from them
Green nodes are tests; the blue node is a macro
Green nodes are errors; the blue node is a passing model
There is no meaningful difference between the colors
questions.explain: Green source nodes have no upstream dependency of their own; the blue model node depends on them via source() calls.

questions.q: Why declare a source instead of just querying the raw table directly by its hardcoded name?
options: It shows up in the Lineage graph, can be tested, and supports freshness checks
There is no difference — declaring a source changes nothing
It makes the query run faster in the warehouse
It's required by Snowflake's security model
questions.explain: Declaring a source makes it visible in the lineage graph, testable with generic tests, and eligible for freshness checks — none of which apply to a bare hardcoded table reference.

options: source() points at raw, un-modeled data; ref() points at another dbt model that dbt itself builds
source() and ref() are two names for the exact same function
ref() only works in tests, source() only works in models
source() is only available in dbt Cloud, not dbt Core
questions.explain: Both are dependency functions resolved by dbt, but source() targets raw data with no upstream dbt dependency, while ref() targets another model.
